Field heterogeneity and neighbours

Alternatives are not FOSS and/or lack documentation and/or features

text:
Four questions to ask of every design



Question
Argument




What moves?
swap, linked_cols*


Where is it allowed to move to?
swap_within


What should it be balanced across?
spatial_factors


What counts as a ‘neighbour’?

*: optional

Every design in this workshop is an answer to these four questions. Refer back to this slide for each new design: CRD, RCBD, split-plot, MET.

title: Spatially optimised experimental designs with speed
text:
The default objective

Adjacency: penalises the same treatment in neighbouring plots (what counts as a neighbour?)
Balance: penalises a treatment repeating in the same rows or columns (what should it be balanced across?)
Minimise the (optionally weighted) sum of these two components

title: Spatially optimised experimental designs with speed
text:
p-rep: optimise

prep_result <- speed(prep_design,
                     swap = "entry",
                     spatial_factors = ~ block + row + col,
                     seed = 42)

Optimising level: single entry within whole design 
Level: single entry within whole design Iteration: 1000 Score: 3.41703 Best: 3.41703 Since Improvement: 0 
Level: single entry within whole design Iteration: 2000 Score: 3.29703 Best: 3.29703 Since Improvement: 27 
Level: single entry within whole design Iteration: 3000 Score: 3.29703 Best: 3.29703 Since Improvement: 1027 
Early stopping at iteration 3973 for level single entry within whole design 



No initialise_ helper needed: any data frame with row/col works. Block in spatial_factors balances the duplicated entries across blocks.
Why not swap_within = “block”? That restricts swaps to within a block, so which entries sit in which block is frozen at whatever the starting layout happened to be. Here the starting layout has both replicates of every two-replicate variety in the same block (0/30 split across blocks), and swap_within = “block” leaves it that way. With block in spatial_factors the balance score penalises uneven block membership, so entries move between blocks: 30/30 varieties end up with one replicate in each block. Blocks in a p-rep are incomplete, so there is no “every treatment once per block” to protect; contrast the RCBD, where blocks start complete and swap_within keeps them complete.

MET Part 2

met_result <- speed(
  data = met_design,
  swap = "treatment",
  optimise = optimise,
  grid_factors = list(dim1 = "row", dim2 = "col", by = "site"),
  early_stop_iterations = 5000,
  optimise_params = optim_params(random_initialisation = TRUE, adj_weight = 0),
  seed = 112, quiet = TRUE
)


grid_factors by says each site is its own grid: plots at different sites are never neighbours. Without it, sites reusing coordinates are refused.

Relationship matrices
Treat related entries as partial repeats when scoring adjacency.

items  <- paste0("T", 1:16)
groups <- setNames(rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), each = 4), items)

within <- c(A = 0.8, B = 0.4, C = 0.1, D = 0.0)
for (g in names(within)) rel[items[groups == g], 
items[groups == g]] <- within[[g]]

title: Spatially optimised experimental designs with speed
text:
Relationship matrices: the effect






















Tiles show each treatment’s relationship group (A: highly related, D: unrelated) not treatment.

Both runs use seed 42. Group A (similarity 0.8) is pushed apart the most; group D (0.0) is free to sit together, which is why D tiles still touch.
Measured on this design (related pairs among neighbours, weighted by the matrix): default 6.8, with the relationship matrix 0.0. Over 20 seeds the means are 7.3 and 0.0.
The final scores are identical (4.27) in both runs: neither has any same-treatment neighbours, and both reach the same balance score. So the score alone does not show the difference; the relationship only changes which layouts count as good, not how good the best one scores.

title: Spatially optimised experimental designs with speed
section: Custom objectives: every pair together 3 times
text:
Custom objectives: every pair together 3 times

T1 and T2 share a block exactly 3 times, like every other pair.

Each column is a block of three plots. T1 and T2 sit together in blocks 1, 5 and 10 (in the seed-42 run); every other pair of the five treatments does the same number of times (lambda = 3). With the default objective the pair counts vary between 2 and 4.

title: Spatially optimised experimental designs with speed
text:
Gotchas

Treatment column not called treatment? Pass treatments = to autoplot()
Companion columns (variety names) don’t move unless named in linked_cols
MET sites reuse coordinates: set grid_factors = list(..., by = "site")
Check summary() flags: a run that hit the iteration cap may need more iterations

title: Exercises
section: Exercise 1: a spatially balanced block design with two-dimensional blocks (about 10 minutes)
text:
Exercise 1: a spatially balanced block design with two-dimensional blocks (about 10 minutes)
Eight varieties, four replicates, in a 4 × 8 field. Instead of whole rows, each block is a 2 × 4 patch of plots.

Set up the layout with initialise_design_df(). Look at the block column.
Optimise it so that treatments only move within their block.
Plot it, then check with table() that every block contains every variety once.

Before you run it, write down your answers to the four questions.


Solution
sbbd <- initialise_design_df(
  items = paste0("V", 1:8), nrows = 4, ncols = 8,
  block_nrows = 2, block_ncols = 4
)
sbbd_opt <- speed(sbbd, swap = "treatment", swap_within = "block", seed = 1)
autoplot(sbbd_opt)
table(sbbd_opt$design_df$block, sbbd_opt$design_df$treatment)


If you finish early, compare how often a variety repeats in the same row or column (table(row, treatment)) with and without spatial_factors = ~ block + row + col.

title: Exercises
text:
Exercise 2: a split-plot (about 10 minutes)
Four tillage methods (whole plots, A to D) and three varieties (subplots, a to c), in three blocks. Each whole plot is a 1 × 3 strip of three subplots, and each block holds four whole plots in a 4 × 3 patch.

Describe the structure with a splits list and build it with initialise_split_design_df(). The blocks are stacked on top of each other (rep_dim).
Write the optimise list: one entry per level, answering the four questions for each. Whole plots must move as a unit.
Plot both levels, then check with table() that every block has every tillage method once, and every whole plot has every variety once.

Hint: the slides’ example has the same shape. Which numbers change?


Solution
splits <- list(
  subplot   = list(items = letters[1:3], nrows = 1, ncols = 1),
  wholeplot = list(items = LETTERS[1:4], nrows = 1, ncols = 3),
  block     = list(nrows = 4, ncols = 3)
)
sp <- initialise_split_design_df(splits = splits, rep_dim = c(3, 1))

optimise <- list(
  wp = list(
    swap        = "wholeplot_treatment",
    swap_within = "block",
    swap_all    = TRUE
  ),
  sp = list(
    swap        = "subplot_treatment",
    swap_within = "wholeplot"
  )
)
sp_opt <- speed(sp, optimise = optimise, seed = 1)

autoplot(sp_opt, treatments = "wholeplot_treatment")
autoplot(sp_opt, treatments = "subplot_treatment", block = "wholeplot")

table(sp_opt$design_df$block, sp_opt$design_df$wholeplot_treatment)
table(sp_opt$design_df$wholeplot, sp_opt$design_df$subplot_treatment)


If you finish early, add a column giving each variety a name (for example "Scepter", "Vixen", "Calibre") and use linked_cols so the names stay with their codes. See the linked_cols section of the main vignette.
